stories.title: Private equity faces existential crisis in US as unsold companies pile up
stories.summary: Private equity firms and the companies they own employ over 13 million, from startups to rural hospitals and large retailers, but experts’ concerns of collapse are growing Retail stalwarts Saks and Eddie Bauer filed for bankruptcy. Kmart and JoAnn Fabrics are gone for good, a trail of layoffs and disappointed customers in their wake. Hospital giant Steward Health Care collapsed, costing thousands of jobs and leaving several communities without a local hospital. These once-trusted US companies have one thing in common: they were owned by private equity investors, who load companies with debt when they buy them and squeeze out profits as they restructure. stories.title: 'Moroccans are desperate: Years of political crackdown and lack of economic opportunities'
stories.summary: François Picard is pleased to welcome Aida Alami, New York Times World contributor. Drawing on her own field reporting at the Moroccan border, Alami challenges attempts to explain the mass crossing primarily through a theory of deliberate state orchestration. While acknowledging both Morocco’s history of leveraging migration in its relations with Spain and the possibility that security forces made tactical decisions on the day, Alami insists on distinguishing evidence from inference. Her reporting instead points toward an interaction between online misinformation, overwhelmed security forces, and a population already primed to migrate by political repression and limited economic opportunity.

stories.title: Isle of May puffin numbers plummet after extreme weather
stories.summary: Puffin numbers in one of the UK's largest colonies have suffered after a drop in food supplies and extreme weather conditions, conservationists have warned. NatureScot said the number of burrows occupied by the seabirds on the Isle of May in the Firth of Forth had fallen by 30% in the last two years. A joint survey also involving the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH) suggested violent storms had killed a number of the birds, while rising ocean temperatures had seriously harmed populations of sand eels - their main source of food. Researchers described the population decline as "disappointing and concerning". About 36,500 burrows on the island – about 4.9 miles (8km) off the coast of Fife - were found to be in active use during the study carried out over the summer. That marked a drop of nearly a third from the 52,000 burrows thought to be in use during the last survey of its kind in 2024. The Isle of May has been a national nature reserve (NNR) since 1956 and has been home to almost 300 species of birds. The reserve's manager, David Steel, said the drop was reminiscent of the early 2000s, when puffin numbers fell before recovering in the 2010s. "The decrease appears to be linked to a combination of ongoing pressures on seabird food supplies, poor winter survival and increasingly extreme weather conditions," he said. "All of this underlines the importance of continued monitoring and conservation work at sites like the Isle of May NNR, where data and research are playing a vital role in helping us to understand these trends and respond." The survey involved researchers sweeping back and forth across the island over a six-day period, counting burrows and assessing whether they were used by puffins or rabbits. The island is also home to guillemots, fulmars, terns and gulls, thanks to its lack of predators.

stories.title: Russia develops Svarog 12 EW roof box system to protect civilian vehicles from drones
stories.summary: The system creates a protective zone around the vehicle and helps reduce the risk of air attacks
article_sentences: MOSCOW, September 4.
Russia has begun deploying the Svarog 12 vehicle-mounted electronic warfare (EW) system to protect civilian vehicles from drones, the Svarog Research and Production Center told TASS.
"In frontline areas, there has been an increase in attacks by Ukrainian drones on civilian vehicles.
In response, production of the Svarog 12 mobile EW system was launched.
The system is compactly placed in a rooftop cargo carrier and does not draw undue attention to the vehicle.
Currently, the 12-channel model with a power output of 50 W has already been put into service," the company noted.
The system creates a protective zone around the vehicle and helps reduce the risk of air attacks.
"Our goal was to create an effective countermeasure against UAVs at a very affordable price.
The Svarog 12 jams drone control channels and blocks the current frequency spectrum used in unmanned systems.
The jamming bands are 300-3,300 MHz and 5,800+ MHz; the device provides protection against FPV drones, cargo drones, and fixed-wing drones," the company added.
